questions.question: What kind of algorithm is **Logistic Regression**, the Case 0 model?
options: A classification algorithm, despite the name
A regression algorithm that predicts a continuous number
A clustering algorithm
A decision tree with a logistic split rule
questions.explanation: Despite the name, Logistic Regression is a **classification** algorithm. It outputs a probability per class through an S-curve (the sigmoid) and predicts the class whose probability is above the threshold, 0.5 by default.

questions.question: How does Logistic Regression turn its input into a probability between 0 and 1?
options: With an S-shaped curve, the sigmoid
By taking a majority vote of the nearest neighbours
By counting the training rows in each leaf
By dividing by the largest feature value
questions.explanation: Logistic Regression computes a linear combination of the features and squeezes it through the sigmoid, which maps any number to a value between 0 and 1. That value is the probability of class 1.

questions.question: Which formula does Linear Regression use to predict?
options: ŷ = intercept + Σ coefficient × feature
ŷ = majority vote of the k closest points
ŷ = 1 / (1 + e^(−feature))
ŷ = the most common class in the training set
questions.explanation: Linear Regression fits a straight line (or plane) through the data: the intercept plus each feature times its coefficient. It assumes the relationship between features and target is linear.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The data lies exactly on y = 2x + 1. `intercept_` is the prediction when the feature is 0 (1.0) and `coef_` is how much the prediction rises per unit of the feature (2.0).

questions.question: What does the **intercept** (`model.intercept_`) of a linear regression mean?
options: The predicted value when all features are 0
How much the prediction changes per unit of a feature
The average error of the model
The share of the variance the model explains
questions.explanation: The intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis: the prediction when every feature is 0. The per-unit change is the coefficient; the share of explained variance is R².

questions.question: A linear model predicting a grade has coefficient 0.3 for `study_hours`. What does that mean?
options: One extra study hour raises the predicted grade by 0.3, with the other features held constant
Study hours explain 30 % of the grade
30 % of the students study enough to pass
Studying one hour more makes the student 0.3 times as likely to pass
questions.explanation: A coefficient (regressiecoëfficiënt) is how much the prediction changes when that feature increases by one unit, with all other features held constant. It describes the model's prediction, not a proven cause.

questions.question: A model has coefficient 5.0 for `hours` (range 1-10) and 0.2 for `income_eur` (range 20 000-80 000). What can you conclude about which feature matters more?
options: Nothing yet: coefficients are only comparable when the features are on the same scale
`hours` matters 25 times more than `income_eur`
`income_eur` matters more because its values are larger
Both matter equally because both coefficients are positive
questions.explanation: A coefficient is per unit of its feature, and one euro is a much smaller step than one hour. 0.2 × 60 000 euros of range is a far bigger effect than 5 × 9 hours. Standardise the features first if you want to compare coefficients.

questions.question: Which description fits a **Decision Tree** (`DecisionTreeClassifier`)?
options: Splits the data with yes/no questions on features; easy to explain, but overfits easily when deep
Many trees on random subsets of the data that take a majority vote
Classifies a point by the majority of its k closest training points
Finds the boundary with the largest margin between the classes
questions.explanation: A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions such as "hours > 4.5?". You can read the rules, which makes it easy to explain, but a deep tree can memorise the training data. The other options describe Random Forest, k-NN and SVM.

questions.question: How does a **Random Forest** compare to a single decision tree?
options: Usually more robust, because many trees on random subsets vote, but less explainable
Easier to explain, because it has fewer rules
Always faster to train
Identical, but with a random `random_state`
questions.explanation: A Random Forest trains many decision trees on random subsets of rows and features and lets them take a majority vote. Averaging out individual trees' mistakes makes it more robust, but you can no longer read one simple set of rules.

questions.question: How does **k-Nearest Neighbors** (`KNeighborsClassifier`) classify a new point?
options: By a majority vote of the k closest training points
By fitting a straight line through the data
By asking yes/no questions on the features
By averaging the predictions of k decision trees
questions.explanation: k-NN looks up the k training points closest to the new point (by distance) and predicts their most common class. It is distance-based, which is why it is very sensitive to feature scale.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: For 4 the three closest points are 3, 2 and 1, all class 0. For 9 they are 10, 11 and 12, all class 1.

questions.question: What happens when you run this?
options: `ValueError`
questions.explanation: k-NN needs k neighbours, but the training set has only 3 rows. `predict()` raises a `ValueError` ("Expected n_neighbors <= n_samples_fit"). The lesson warns about this when you swap in `KNeighborsClassifier` on the tiny Case 0 dataset: k must not exceed the number of training rows.

questions.question: What does a **Support Vector Machine** (SVM) look for?
options: The boundary with the largest margin between the classes
The k closest training points
The feature that best splits the data in two
The straight line with the smallest squared error
questions.explanation: An SVM finds the decision boundary that leaves the widest gap (margin) between the classes. Like k-NN it works with distances, so it is also sensitive to feature scale.

questions.question: Case 0's features are on different scales (hours ~1-10, exercises ~5-35). Which assignment model does **not** care about that?
options: `DecisionTreeClassifier`
`KNeighborsClassifier`
An SVM
None of them; every model needs scaled features
questions.explanation: A tree splits on one feature at a time with a threshold ("exercises > 17?"), and rescaling a feature just moves the threshold. k-NN and SVM compute distances across features, so the feature with the larger range dominates unless you scale.
